papers.title: Impact of expanded influenza vaccination programs in children and adults in Australia: a mathematical modelling study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368629 v1

summary.one_liner: A mathematical model calibrated to Australian surveillance data compares live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) programs for school-aged children against expanded inactivated vaccine (IIV) uptake in adults, measuring impact per dose given.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how best to use flu vaccines in Australia, where most current programs focus on protecting older adults. The researchers built a computer simulation of how flu spreads and gets vaccinated, checked it against real surveillance data, and compared a nasal-spray vaccine for children with strategies that get more adults vaccinated with the injected vaccine. They found the children's program was estimated to prevent the most hospital stays and deaths overall, though it was not the most efficient option for adults aged 65 and over.
summary.why: Flu causes serious illness each year, and this study tests whether a newer vaccine type could add to existing programs. The results are model estimates, not trial outcomes, so they depend on the assumptions built into the simulation; the abstract alone does not show how sensitive they are.
summary.background:
- Influenza (flu) is a common virus causing severe illness, especially in young children and older adults.
- Inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV) is the standard injected flu shot, mainly used to protect older adults in Australia.
- Live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is a weakened live-virus vaccine, given as a nasal spray, now approved for children aged 2 to 17.
- Mathematical modelling uses computer simulations of how infection spreads through a population, here calibrated (tuned) to surveillance data, which are routine records of cases and hospitalisations.
- "Dose efficiency" means how much health benefit each vaccine dose delivers.
- "Number needed to vaccinate" (NNV) is how many people must be vaccinated to prevent one hospitalisation; a higher number means less efficient.
- Coverage is the share of the target group that is vaccinated.

papers.abstract: Background: Seasonal influenza is a common cause of severe illness, particularly in young children and older adults. In Australia, influenza vaccination programs using the inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV) largely focus on direct protection of older adults. Live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is now available for children aged 2-17 years, offering an opportunity to complement existing IIV programs. Methods: We developed a mathematical model of seasonal influenza transmission and vaccination in Australia, calibrated to surveillance data. We evaluated the health impact of LAIV programs on influenza burden relative to a baseline IIV-only scenario that assumed current coverage levels. We compared the dose efficiency of LAIV programs targeting school-aged children with strategies that increased IIV uptake in adults. Findings: An LAIV program targeting children aged 5-17 years was estimated to have the largest population-level impact, reducing influenza hospitalisations by 16% and deaths by 13%, assuming 55% coverage. An IIV program achieving 55% coverage in adults aged 50 years and older was predicted to have a similar population-level reduction in hospitalisations to a primary school-aged LAIV program (around 9.5%). Based only on doses administered, LAIV programs were more efficient at averting cases, hospitalisations, and deaths than strategies that expanded IIV uptake in adults. However, for outcomes in adults [≥]65 years old, increasing IIV uptake in this age group was estimated to be the most efficient strategy, with a number needed to vaccinate of 1811 to avert one hospitalisation. Interpretation: Our results support the potential use of LAIV as an additional tool in the prevention of seasonal influenza in Australia.

papers.title: Distinct pulmonary transcriptomic and proteomic host signatures enable accurate diagnosis of severe lower respiratory tract infection
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368772 v1

summary.one_liner: Paired transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of tracheal aspirates from critically ill children shows that RNA and protein measurements converge on similar immune pathways and give similarly accurate LRTI classifiers, despite poor gene-protein correlation.
summary.plain: Lower respiratory tract infections, such as pneumonia in the lungs and airways, can be hard to tell apart from non-infectious illness in very sick children. This study took samples from the airways of 105 critically ill children and measured both their gene activity (RNA) and their proteins. Both measurements pointed to a similar infection pattern, and both could identify infection with similarly high accuracy, though they picked out different key markers.
summary.why: It addresses whether it is better to measure RNA or proteins when looking for the body's immune response to infection, which matters for designing future diagnostic tests. The findings are from a single study of 105 children, so how far they generalise to other settings is not established by the text.
summary.background:
- Lower respiratory tract infection: infection of the lungs and airways, such as pneumonia or bronchiolitis.
- Tracheal aspirate: a sample of fluid suctioned from the windpipe of a patient on breathing support.
- Transcriptomics: measuring which genes are active, via their RNA messages.
- Proteomics: measuring the proteins present in a sample, which carry out most of the body's work.
- Gene-protein correlation: whether a gene's RNA level tracks its protein level; poor agreement means the two measure partly different things.
- Classifier and AUC: a computer model that sorts patients into groups; AUC (area under the curve) near 1 means very accurate, and above 0.90 is high.
- Host signature: a pattern in the patient's own immune response, used as an alternative to detecting the microbe itself.

papers.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) is a leading cause of acute respiratory illness, yet distinguishing it from noninfectious conditions remains a clinical challenge. Measuring the host immune response in the blood or lower airways, rather than exclusively detecting pathogens, has emerged as an alternative diagnostic strategy. However, it remains unclear whether RNA or protein measurements yield greater diagnostic information, or whether the two capture the same underlying biology. To address this, we performed paired transcriptomics and proteomics on tracheal aspirate specimens from 105 critically ill children with respiratory failure, 72 with microbiologically confirmed LRTI and 33 with noninfectious causes. Both approaches detected a clear host signature of LRTI which converged on similar core immune pathways including interferon signaling, inflammation, and complement activation. Despite this, agreement between individual genes and their corresponding proteins was largely poor. Diagnostic classifiers built from either RNA or protein data identified LRTI with similarly high accuracy (AUC>0.90), but selected different top biomarkers, and yielded discordant classifications for 12% of patients. Taken together, we find that lower airway transcriptomics and proteomics capture similar global biological features of LRTI despite poor correlation between gene and protein expression, providing fresh insight into approaches for biomarker discovery and clinical translation.

papers.title: Efficacy, Immunogenicity, and Safety of an Inactivated Bivalent EV-A71-CVA16 Vaccine in Children: A Randomized Phase 3 Trial
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368796 v1

summary.background:
- Hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD): a viral infection causing fever, blisters on hands, feet and mouth, mostly in young children.
- Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) and coxsackievirus A16 (CVA16): two viruses that are major causes of HFMD.
- Inactivated vaccine: a vaccine made from virus particles killed so they cannot replicate, but still able to trigger immunity.
- Bivalent vaccine: a single vaccine containing two strains or types of target.
- Randomized, double-blind trial: participants are assigned to groups by chance and neither they nor the researchers know which vaccine is given.
- Vaccine efficacy: the percentage reduction in cases among vaccinated versus control participants.
- Seroconversion and geometric mean titer (GMT): measures of antibody response; seroconversion is the share of people who develop detectable antibodies, and GMT is the average antibody level on a log scale.
- Noninferiority: showing a new vaccine is not meaningfully worse than an existing one.
- RT-PCR: a lab test that detects viral genetic material.
summary.one_liner: A randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial in 8,000 children aged 6-71 months reports that a bivalent inactivated EV-A71/CVA16 vaccine met its prespecified efficacy endpoint against CVA16-associated hand, foot and mouth disease and its noninferiority endpoint for EV-A71 immunogenicity versus a licensed EV-A71 vaccine.
summary.plain: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a common illness in young children, caused mainly by two viruses, EV-A71 and CVA16. This trial gave a new vaccine that targets both viruses at once to thousands of children, and compared it with a vaccine already licensed against EV-A71 alone. The reported results suggest the two-dose vaccine protected against CVA16 illness and produced antibody responses against EV-A71 that were at least as good as the licensed vaccine.
summary.why: Currently licensed vaccines cover only EV-A71, so CVA16 has been a gap in protection; a single product covering both viruses could address that. The text reports only the trial's own results, and the efficacy estimate rests on a small number of cases (4 versus 44), so the findings should be seen as preliminary until independent confirmation and longer follow-up are available.

papers.abstract: Background Enterovirus A71 (EVA71) and coxsackievirus A16 (CVA16) cause hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). We evaluated the efficacy, immunogenicity, and safety of a bivalent EVA71-CVA16 vaccine. Methods In this multicenter, double-blind, phase 3 trial, 8,000 healthy children aged 6-71 months were randomly assigned (1:1) to two doses of the bivalent or a licensed EVA71 vaccine, 1 month apart. The primary efficacy endpoint was RT-PCR-confirmed CVA16-associated HFMD with onset at least 14 days after dose 2. EVA71 immunogenicity noninferiority was assessed among baseline-seronegative participants without previous EVA71 vaccination. Results Of 7,975 participants receiving at least one dose, 7,419 underwent the primary efficacy analysis. CVA16-associated HFMD occurred in 4 bivalent-group versus 44 EVA71-group participants (vaccine efficacy, 90.91%; 95% CI, 75.03-97.63). At 30 days after dose 2, the EVA71 geometric mean titer (GMT) ratio was 2.04 (95% CI, 1.71-2.44) among baseline-seronegative participants without previous EVA71 vaccination. In the humoral immunogenicity population at this time point, CVA16 seroconversion rates were 96.94% versus 8.68%, and GMTs were 918.96 versus 3.88 U/mL. Adverse reactions within 30 days after either dose occurred in 46.73% versus 36.07% of reactogenicity-subgroup participants. In the overall safety population, serious adverse events occurred in 6.22% versus 7.55% from dose 1 through 6 months after dose 2; one bivalent-group event was considered possibly vaccine-related. No deaths occurred. Conclusions The bivalent EVA71-CVA16 vaccine met the prespecified efficacy criterion against CVA16-associated HFMD and the EVA71 immunogenicity noninferiority criterion in children aged 6-71 months (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06734832).

papers.title: Deep Learning-based Phylodynamic Inference of Oropouche Virus Transmission Dynamics in Brazil Between 2023 and 2025
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.26368826 v1

summary.background:
- Phylodynamics: inferring how an epidemic spreads by analysing the family tree (phylogeny) of viral genome sequences.
- Birth-death model: a standard statistical model of how lineages branch and die out over time, used here as a baseline.
- Reproduction number (R): the average number of new infections caused by one infected individual; here R_HH is the human-to-human value over one full human-vector-human cycle.
- Vector: an organism, such as a midge or mosquito, that carries the pathogen between hosts.
- Incubation period (exposed stage): the time between being infected and becoming able to transmit.
- Reassortant lineage: a virus strain formed when segments of its genome mix with another strain.
- Endemic vs non-endemic: whether a disease is regularly present in a region versus newly appearing there.
- Deep learning: machine-learning methods using layered neural networks, here used to make the inference.
summary.one_liner: A deep-learning phylodynamic model (BDEIVH) that explicitly represents alternating human-vector transmission and incubation is applied to Oropouche virus genomic clusters in Brazil (2023–2025), estimating vector and human infection durations and reproduction numbers.
summary.plain: Oropouche virus, spread by biting midges and mosquitoes, caused a large outbreak across the Americas from 2023 to 2025. The authors built a computer model that tracks how the virus passes back and forth between people and insects, and used it to read the family trees of viral genomes collected in Brazil. They report that the model estimates the virus spread more accurately than standard models in simulated tests, and that each infected person typically passed it on to about 1.15 to 1.81 others across the three main Brazilian clusters.
summary.why: Understanding how fast a vector-borne virus spreads in both endemic and non-endemic areas can inform surveillance and control planning. The text does not describe any public-health intervention or validation against field case counts, so its practical impact is not established from this text alone.

papers.abstract: Oropouche virus caused an unprecedented epidemic across the Americas during 2023-2025, associated with the expansion of the reassortant M1L2S2 lineage. To investigate its dissemination, we develop the Birth-Death Exposed-Infectious Vector-Human (BDEIVH) model within a deep-learning framework that explicitly represents alternating human-vector transmission and incubation periods. The model defines two directional reproduction numbers, RVH and RHV, whose product, RHH, quantifies the expected number of secondary human infections generated by a single infectious human through one complete transmission cycle. In simulations, BDEIVH provides more accurate RHH estimates than conventional birth-death models, with predictive accuracy improving with phylogeny size and remaining robust under reduced phylogenetic resolution. Across three major Brazilian OROV genomic clusters, estimated durations of infection range from 15.4 to 18.5 days in vectors and from 9.42 to 12.3 days in humans, whereas whole-cluster RHH estimates range from 1.15 to 1.81. RHH estimates reached a peak of 4.4 in the endemic Amazon region and 3.0 in the non-endemic Atlantic Forest region. These findings show that explicitly modelling vector-mediated transmission improves phylodynamic inference and reveals substantial OROV transmission in both endemic and non-endemic regions.

papers.title: Pre-conception PfSPZ Vaccine administration to Malian women prevents malaria in their offspring during infancy
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368501 v1

summary.background:
- Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, spread by mosquitoes; Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous species.
- PfSPZ Vaccine is made of live but attenuated (weakened) parasite sporozoites, the stage that enters the body from a mosquito bite.
- "Pre-conception" means given before pregnancy begins.
- "Parasitemia" means malaria parasites detected in the blood, often via a blood smear under a microscope.
- "Vaccine efficacy (VE)" is the percentage reduction in cases among vaccinated versus control groups; a wide confidence interval (CI) means the estimate is uncertain.
- Placebo-controlled and double-blind means neither participants nor researchers knew who got the real vaccine.
- PfCSP antibodies are immune proteins against the parasite's circumsporozoite protein, measured as a sign of immune response.
summary.one_liner: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial in Mali testing whether pre-conception PfSPZ malaria vaccination of women reduces parasitemia and clinical malaria in their infants during the first year of life.
summary.plain: Malaria is especially dangerous for babies and pregnant women, and protecting infants is hard. In this trial in Mali, healthy women were given either a malaria vaccine (at one of two doses) or saline before they became pregnant, and their babies were then tracked for malaria during the first year of life. In the lower-dose vaccine group, far fewer infants had malaria parasites in their blood or clinical malaria than in the saline group, while the higher-dose group did not show a significant effect.
summary.why: Protecting infants through a vaccine given to mothers before pregnancy would be a new approach if it holds up, which is why it merits attention. The sample is small (104 infants, with wide confidence intervals), and the higher-dose group did not show a significant benefit, so the result should be read as promising rather than settled.

papers.abstract: Background: Preconception administration of Plasmodium falciparum sporozoite (PfSPZ) Vaccine is safe and prevents malaria during pregnancies identified within 21 months post-vaccination. We evaluated pre-conception PfSPZ Vaccine effects on malaria risk in offspring during the first year of life. Methods: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Ouelessebougou, Mali, 300 healthy 18-38-year-old women were allocated 1:1:1 to receive 9x10^5 PfSPZ or 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ of PfSPZ Vaccine or normal saline on days 1-8-29, and followed up to 21 months for malaria endpoints and pregnancies. 104 infants from 103 pregnancies identified first year post-vaccination [9x10^5 PfSPZ (n=38); 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ (n=40); normal saline (n=26)] were seen every two months and during illnesses. Primary endpoints were blood-smear parasitemia and clinical malaria. Safety outcomes included newborn baseline characteristics and infant adverse events (AEs). Findings: Newborn baseline characteristics and infant AEs did not differ between arms; AEs were common but predominantly mild (91.9-96% Grade 1). Vaccine efficacy of 9x10^5 PfSPZ was 75.1% (95% CI 20.6-92.2) against parasitemia (10.5% parasitemic infants versus 38.5% of placebo) and 94.2% (54.9-99.3) against clinical malaria (2.6% malarious infants versus 38.5% of placebo). VE of 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ group was 40.3% (-43.6-75.2) against parasitemia and 36.3% (-50.3-73.0) against clinical malaria, both non-significant. At 6 and 12 months of age, PfCSP antibodies were similar in offspring of vaccinated and control mothers. Interpretation: Pre-conception PfSPZ Vaccine was safe and reduced Pf infection and clinical malaria during infancy in 9x10^5 PfSPZ group. Further development of preconception PfSPZ vaccines is warranted to protect mother-infant dyads.

papers.title: Proteome-wide antibody responses to PfSPZ Vaccine include cross-reactive antibodies that correlate with protection from malaria
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367676 v1

summary.background:
- PfSPZ Vaccine: a malaria vaccine made of live but radiation-attenuated sporozoites (the infective form of the Plasmodium falciparum parasite) given to volunteers.
- Antibodies: immune proteins that bind specific molecular targets (antigens); "seropositive" means antibodies to a target were detected in blood serum.
- CSP (circumsporozoite protein): the most abundant surface protein on sporozoites and the main target of the vaccine's antibody response; it has repeated central sequences.
- Proteome-wide arrays: chips carrying most of the parasite's proteins (or overlapping peptide fragments) to test which ones antibodies bind.
- Cross-reactivity: one antibody binding several unrelated targets that share similar sequence pieces.
- Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs): identical antibodies cloned from single immune cells, used to test specific binding.
- Correlate of protection: a measurable immune marker statistically associated with being protected; it does not by itself prove causation.
summary.one_liner: A proteome-wide antibody survey of sera from PfSPZ-vaccinated malaria-naive volunteers finds that antibodies to many non-CSP Plasmodium falciparum proteins, which share sequence homology with CSP's central repeat and junctional regions, correlate with protection and are partly cross-reactive with CSP-targeting monoclonal antibodies.
summary.plain: Malaria vaccine researchers wanted to know which antibodies in people's blood best predict protection after being immunized with a whole-parasite vaccine. They tested volunteers' blood against nearly the entire malaria parasite's set of proteins, using protein and peptide arrays. They found that antibodies aimed at the main vaccine target, CSP, were linked to protection, but so were antibodies that stuck to other parasite proteins with similar sequence fragments.
summary.why: The vaccine is known to protect, but its antibody correlates have mostly been studied for a few antigens, so a broader view could point to new vaccine candidates. The finding that CSP-type antibodies also bind unrelated parasite proteins is unexpected and raises questions about parasite biology and cross-reactivity, though the text does not establish how these off-target bindings affect protection.

papers.abstract: The PfSPZ Vaccine induces both humoral and cellular immunity. While T cells are likely critical for protection, previous analyses of antibody correlates have focused on select antigens. Here, we apply a proteome-wide approach to examine antibody responses across the entire Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) proteome. Sera from malaria-naive volunteers immunized with high doses of PfSPZ Vaccine were probed using whole proteome Pf protein microarrays and high-density Pf peptide microarrays. Both platforms identified antibody responses that significantly correlated with protection, including responses to the immunodominant Pf circumsporozoite protein (CSP). Multiple reactive epitopes within non-CSP proteins shared homology with the central repeat and junctional regions of CSP, suggesting broad intra-proteome cross-reactivity. Greater breadth of seropositive responses was associated with protection. Cross-reactivity was confirmed by off-target binding of well-characterized memory B cell- and plasmablast-derived monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting CSP. What began as a search for antibody correlates of protection and potential vaccine candidate antigens led to the surprising discovery of probable promiscuous CSP antibody responses that bind non-CSP proteins. The association between protection and greater levels of intra- and extra-Plasmodium cross-reactivity raises new questions about parasite biology and microbial evolution.

papers.title: Evaluation of urine lipoarabinomannan and host response signatures for culture-negative tuberculosis using composite criteria and Bayesian Latent Class Analysis
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368340 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial lung infection; culture grows the bacteria in a lab to confirm it.
- "Culture-negative" means the usual lab test did not find the bacteria, even though TB may still be suspected.
- Sensitivity is the share of true cases a test catches; specificity is the share of non-cases it correctly clears.
- A reference standard is the benchmark used to judge a test; without a perfect one, researchers use composite criteria (combining several clinical or lab findings) or latent class analysis (a statistical method that infers hidden true disease status from patterns across tests).
- Bayesian analysis gives a credible interval, the Bayesian counterpart of a confidence interval.
- Urine lipoarabinomannan is a bacterial-cell-wall molecule detected in urine; host transcriptional response signatures are patterns of gene activity in the blood.
- Sample sizes are modest (112 culture-negative and 55 culture-positive adults, plus 17 controls).
summary.one_liner: Compares three ways of defining culture-negative tuberculosis (composite microbiological, composite clinical, and Bayesian latent class model) to estimate how well urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS) detect the disease.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis (TB) is sometimes present even when standard lab culture of sputum (phlegm) comes back negative, and there is no reliable gold-standard test to confirm these cases. This study looked at urine and blood samples from people with suspected TB in Africa and tested two non-sputum tests on them. The main finding is that the three ways of defining the disease sorted people differently, yet the tests' accuracy estimates overlapped enough to lead to similar overall conclusions.
summary.why: Diagnosing TB without sputum culture matters because many people who are ill cannot produce good sputum samples, and better non-sputum tests could help. The paper also shows that how the reference standard is chosen can change the picture, which is relevant to how any new diagnostic is judged.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. Results: Positive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). Conclusion: Three distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB.

papers.title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368138 v1

summary.background:
- Upper respiratory tract: the nose and throat, where many respiratory viruses first enter the body.
- Microbiome: the community of bacteria and other microbes that normally live on body surfaces.
- Human challenge model: a study where volunteers are intentionally infected under controlled conditions, which allows timing of exposure to be known.
- Gene expression: measurement of which genes are switched on in tissue samples, used here as a readout of immune activity.
- Interferon and neutrophil responses: parts of the immune system's early alarm and first-responder activity against viruses and bacteria.
- Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus, Dolosigranulum: genera of common bacteria found in the nose; S. aureus is a species that can cause infections.
- Viral load: the amount of virus measured in a sample.
summary.one_liner: In a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study of 34 healthy young adults (18 infected), baseline nasal and throat microbiome composition and host gene expression were linked to infection susceptibility, symptoms, and viral load.
summary.plain: Researchers looked at why some people catch COVID-19 and others do not, even when exposed to the same virus. In a study where healthy volunteers were deliberately given the virus, they compared the bacteria living in the nose and throat, and the nose's immune activity, before the virus was given. People who later became infected differed modestly in both.
summary.why: The paper suggests that the mix of bacteria in the nose and the local immune state before exposure may relate to who gets infected and how sick they get. These are associations from a small study, so they point toward possible mechanisms rather than establishing cause.

papers.abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.

papers.title: Long-term transmission chains fueling the drug-resistant tuberculosis burden in Southern Brazil
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368293 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a bacterium spread through the air.
- Drug-resistant TB does not respond to some or all standard drugs; rifampicin is a key first-line drug.
- Whole-genome sequencing reads the bacterium's full genetic code, allowing researchers to tell whether cases are closely related.
- A "5-SNP threshold" means genomes differing by five or fewer single-letter genetic changes are grouped as likely linked.
- Drug susceptibility testing comes in two types: genotypic (detecting resistance genes) and phenotypic (growing bacteria with drugs in the lab).
- "Acquired" resistance develops during treatment; "transmitted" resistance is caught from another person.
summary.one_liner: Whole-genome sequencing of 33 new drug-resistant TB isolates plus 267 historical genomes from Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, indicates that transmission between people, including in prisons and communities, drives most rifampicin resistance in the region.
summary.plain: This paper looks at drug-resistant tuberculosis, a lung infection that resists standard antibiotics, in the Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul. The researchers sequenced the bacteria's genomes from recent patients and compared them with older samples to trace how the infection spreads. They found that most resistance came from the disease passing from person to person, rather than from patients becoming resistant during treatment.
summary.why: Tracing transmission chains tells public health teams where to focus case finding, resistance testing and contact tracing, including in prisons. The study covers one region over a limited period, so its findings may not apply directly elsewhere.

papers.abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death, with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) challenging disease control. Brazil has a high TB burden, and Rio Grande do Sul state reports persistently high incidence and drug-resistance rates. The drivers shaping the regional DR-TB burden remain poorly characterised. Methods We conducted genomic surveillance of confirmed DR-TB cases in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, from January 2023 to September 2024. Clinical isolates underwent genotypic (gDST) and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We analyzed 33 newly sequenced genomes and 267 historical Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes collected in 2011-2019 to characterize resistance, transmission, and spatiotemporal patterns and estimate the contributions of transmitted and acquired rifampicin resistance. Findings Molecular testing detected rifampicin resistance missed by pDST, including borderline rpoB mutations in 18.2% and emerging resistance-associated variants in 3% of the 33 analyzed isolates. Conversely, pDST detected baseline bedaquiline resistance missed by WGS in one newly diagnosed case. Among 300 genomes, 181 (60.3%) clustered into 32 genomic clusters at a 5-SNP threshold, including 12 with long-term circulation and several spanning prisons and communities. Sublineage frequencies remained stable over time, whereas we observed marked geographic structuring and localized clonal expansion. Among 178 rifampicin-resistant isolates, transmission accounted for an estimated 79.2-88.2% of resistance, corresponding to 11.8-20.8% of cases arising through de novo acquisition during treatment. Interpretation Our findings identify active transmission as the main driver of rifampicin-resistant TB in Rio Grande do Sul, with long-term transmission chains extending across both incarcerated and community settings. These results underscore the urgent need to strengthen timely TB case detection and resistance testing, enhance contact investigations, and implement targeted interventions aiming to interrupt persistent transmission chains.

papers.title: The effect of smallpox vaccination: unique insights gained from Danish post-honeymoon epidemics 200 years ago
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368180 v1

summary.background:
- Smallpox (caused by the Variola virus) was a deadly disease, especially for children, and was eradicated worldwide in 1980.
- Variola minor is the milder form of the virus; Variola major is the severe form.
- Case fatality ratio (CFR): the share of sick people who die.
- Vaccine effectiveness (VE): how much a vaccine reduces the chance of a bad outcome, here death, compared with the unvaccinated.
- Waning immunity: protection that weakens over time.
- Quarantine: isolating sick people to stop spread.
- Retrospective data: records collected in the past, analysed later.
summary.one_liner: Retrospective analysis of 3,795 Copenhagen smallpox patients (1824–1835) estimating age-specific case fatality and vaccine effectiveness against death, interpreting a milder "post-honeymoon" resurgence as a result of high vaccine coverage plus waning adult protection rather than viral change.
summary.plain: Smallpox was nearly stopped in Copenhagen by 1810, when about 90% of children had been vaccinated, but it returned in 1824 as a milder disease striking adults. This paper uses records from 3,795 patients treated by physicians between 1824 and 1835, when all patients were quarantined, to compare death rates among vaccinated and unvaccinated people. The authors report that the vaccine appeared to prevent most deaths in the first four outbreaks, and that protection seemed to fade with age in the fifth.
summary.why: It offers a rare historical natural experiment on how a vaccine and its waning protection shape which age groups a disease hits and how severe it looks. The authors argue that high vaccination can make a dangerous virus look like a milder one, which may matter for interpreting modern outbreak data, though the text does not spell out such links.

papers.abstract: BackgroundHistorically, the Variola virus caused deadly smallpox epidemics in children. In Copenhagen, transmission was halted by 1810 when [~]90% of children were vaccinated following the introduction of a mandatory single-dose vaccine program. A 14-year honeymoon period followed, but in 1824 smallpox re-emerged as a milder disease of adults. We set out to study smallpox epidemics between 1824 and 1835 when all smallpox patients in Copenhagen were quarantined. MethodWe analyze data from 3795 smallpox patients reported by the treating physicians between 1824 and 1835. The data include age, vaccination status, and outcome. We estimate age-specific case fatality ratios (CFR) and vaccine effectiveness (VE) against mortality. FindingsFor the four outbreaks while quarantine was mandatory (1824-1834), the CFR was [~]1% among the vaccinated and [~]25% among the unvaccinated, corresponding to a VE of [~]95%. For the fifth outbreak in 1835, we found that CFR was low among the vaccinated but increased with age, which is evidence of waning vaccine protection. Almost no cases were over 40 years of age, suggesting lifelong immunity from smallpox infection. InterpretationAs the unvaccinated CFR was high and comparable to the pre-vaccine era, the milder post-honeymoon smallpox disease cannot be explained by genetic changes in the virus. Rather, high coverage with an effective vaccine combined with waning vaccine protection in adulthood explains the changing face of smallpox. We demonstrates how high vaccine coverage can disguise an outbreak of highly pathogenic smallpox as the milder Variola minor.

papers.title: Old lineages, new threat: the re-emergence of pneumococcal serotype 14 in adults in Catalonia, Spain (2023-2025).
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367621 v1

summary.background:
- Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae) is a bacterium that can cause pneumonia, blood infection and meningitis.
- Serotype: a variant of the bacterium defined by its outer sugar coat (capsule); vaccines target specific serotypes.
- Conjugate vaccines: vaccines that train immunity against these capsules; paediatric schedules in recent years use more serotypes ("higher valency").
- Herd protection: indirect protection of unvaccinated people when many others are vaccinated; the paper notes its limits here.
- Lineage / clone: a family of closely related bacteria; GPSC is a naming system for pneumococcal lineages.
- Genotyping methods: PFGE and MLST (older fingerprinting and gene-typing), and whole-genome sequencing by Illumina (newer, more detailed).
- Quellung: a classic microscope-based serotyping test.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective genomic and clinical study of adult invasive pneumococcal disease in Catalonia (1996-2025) reports a 2023-2025 resurgence of vaccine-type serotype 14, driven by several previously circulating lineages rather than one new clone or capsule variant.
summary.plain: Pneumococcal bacteria cause serious infections such as blood infections and pneumonia, and vaccines have cut these infections a lot. This paper looks at a type of these bacteria called serotype 14, which had become rare in adults in the Catalan region of Spain but has become more common again in 2025. The authors compared older bacterial samples with recent ones and looked at patients' health records.
summary.why: Vaccine-covered types coming back in adults is a concern for public health planning, and the paper suggests the rise may reflect general shifts in circulation rather than a new, more dangerous strain. The authors themselves say the causes are uncertain, so the explanations offered are possibilities, not established findings.

papers.abstract: IntroductionThe introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines resulted in a decline in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD). Nevertheless, recent studies report a re-emergence of vaccine-included serotypes. AimTo describe the recent re-emergence of serotype 14 IPD among adults in Catalonia and to investigate the factors underlying its resurgence. MethodsWe analysed two collections of adult IPD isolates: a historical series from Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (1996-2025) and a multicentre series from seven tertiary hospitals in Catalonia (2023-2025). Isolates were serotyped (Quellung) and genotyped by PFGE/MLST (1996-2022) or Illumina sequencing (2023-2025). Clinical data were retrospectively collected. ResultsThe historical series showed that, after peaking in 2009, serotype 14 frequency gradually declined, with only 0-4 cases reported annually between 2016 and 2020. However, the number of serotype 14 isolates increased again in 2025, reaching 11.0% of all isolates at HUB and 10.8% across Catalonia. Genomic data showed that this increase involved multiple previously circulating lineages (GPSC6, GPSC18, GPSC16 and GPSC39), with no dominant clone. Analysis of the capsular locus revealed substantial genetic diversity, with no association between capsular variants and either lineage or year of isolation. A substantial proportion of patients (56.3%) had multiple comorbidities and only 18.8% were appropriately vaccinated. DiscussionThe re-emergence of serotype 14 was not associated with a novel lineage or capsular variant. Instead, it may reflect a combination of post-pandemic transmission changes, higher-valency paediatric vaccines, and natural fluctuations in serotype circulation. These findings highlight the limits of herd protection and underscore the need to strengthen adult vaccination, particularly among at-risk populations.

papers.title: Frequency and antibiotic susceptibility of urinary Klebsiella in Lahore
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368163 v1

summary.background:
- Urinary tract infection (UTI): an infection of the urinary system, usually by bacteria that enter the bladder.
- Klebsiella: a group of bacteria, including the species K. pneumoniae and K. oxytoca, that can cause UTIs and other infections.
- Antibiotic susceptibility: whether a bacterial sample is killed or held back by a given antibiotic in lab testing; "susceptible" means it responds, "resistant" means it does not.
- Isolate: one bacterial sample grown from one patient's specimen.
- Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem): strong, broad-spectrum antibiotics often kept for serious infections.
- Cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides: other antibiotic families mentioned as frequently ineffective here.
- Limitation: the paper reports results for 18 isolates per drug in aggregate, and notes species-level susceptibility was not verified.
summary.one_liner: A small single-hospital study from Lahore, Pakistan (95 urine samples, July–December 2023) reporting how often Klebsiella bacteria caused urinary infections and how susceptible those isolates were to common antibiotics.
summary.plain: Urinary tract infections are often caused by bacteria that respond differently to different antibiotics, so doctors need local data to choose treatment. The authors examined urine samples from 95 patients at one hospital in Lahore and found bacteria grew in 63 of them. Among these, 18 were Klebsiella, and the lab tests suggested that imipenem and meropenem worked against almost all of those 18 isolates.
summary.why: Rising antibiotic resistance is a worldwide concern, and local resistance patterns help show which drugs may still work. However, the sample is small, from a single hospital, and the authors themselves say the results are not yet reliable enough to guide local treatment policy.

papers.abstract: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings.1 We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023. Urine culture showed significant bacterial growth in 63 specimens (66.3%). Escherichia coli accounted for 30 isolates, followed by 18 Klebsiella isolates, comprising 16 Klebsiella pneumoniae and two Klebsiella oxytoca. Klebsiella was recovered from 12 female and six male patients, and the largest number of Klebsiella isolates occurred in patients aged 21-30 years. The aggregate susceptibility results, recorded for 18 isolates per antibiotic, showed the highest susceptibility to imipenem and meropenem (17/18 each), followed by nitrofurantoin (16/18). Resistance to several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides was frequent. These findings describe the bacterial distribution and reported susceptibility patterns in a small hospital sample. Larger studies with verified species-specific susceptibility data are needed before these findings can guide local treatment policy.

papers.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis: unmasking population diversity and antimicrobial resistance in the Australian context
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367559 v1

summary.background:
- Bronchiectasis: a long-term lung disease in which damaged airways become widened and clogged with mucus, making chronic infection likely.
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a common, hard-to-kill bacterium that often colonises damaged lungs.
- Antimicrobial resistance (AMR): when bacteria survive drugs meant to kill them; multidrug-resistant means resistant to several drug classes, and extremely drug-resistant means resistant to nearly all available options.
- Whole-genome sequencing: reading the complete DNA of a bacterium to trace relationships between strains.
- Sequence type (ST): a standard label for a bacterial lineage based on a few housekeeping genes; "high-risk international clones" are lineages widely linked to resistance and spread.
- Within-host evolution and persistence: the bacterium changing and staying in one patient over years.
- Mobile genetic elements: pieces of DNA that can move between bacteria and carry resistance genes; the authors found none of the high-risk type here.
summary.one_liner: Genomic and antimicrobial susceptibility study of 137 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis, compared against 4,575 public bronchiectasis-derived genomes.
summary.plain: People with bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition where the airways are widened and scarred, often carry a bacterium called Pseudomonas aeruginosa that is hard to treat. This study collected bacterial samples from 59 Australian patients over 2009 to 2025, tested how well they resisted common antibiotics, and read their full genetic code. The authors then compared these bacteria with thousands of publicly available genomes from other bronchiectasis patients.
summary.why: The reported resistance levels are high, with about three-quarters of isolates resistant to at least one drug, which matters for treatment choices in a group the authors describe as neglected. The findings are limited to one country's small clinical sample, so they describe Australian patients rather than establishing wider trends.

papers.abstract: BackgroundPseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. MethodsP. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. ResultsHigh AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. ConclusionsOur study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.

papers.title: Genomic diversity of respiratory pathogens in clinical versus community surveillance: a comparative analysis of SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza viruses in Washington State
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.26367863 v1

summary.background:
- Genomic surveillance: sequencing viral genomes from samples to see which lineages (clades) are circulating and how they change.
- Clade: a group of closely related viral lineages, named by convention (e.g., 21J = Delta, 22B = Omicron BA.5).
- Clinical vs community samples: clinical samples come from people seeking care; community samples come from people enrolled in studies regardless of symptoms.
- Non-synonymous mutation: a genetic change that alters the protein built from it; spike-protein changes can affect antibody binding.
- Monoclonal antibody: a lab-made antibody treatment; resistance means a variant evades it.
- Ct value: PCR cycle threshold; lower values generally mean more virus in the sample.
- RSV: respiratory syncytial virus, a common cause of winter respiratory illness, especially in young children and older adults.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective comparison of whole-genome sequences of SARS-CoV-2, RSV and influenza from clinical (health-care-seeking) and community-based surveillance samples in Washington State, examining clade proportions, cluster diversity, spike mutations and viral load (Ct values).
summary.plain: Public health teams track how viruses change by sequencing their genetic code, but most of these samples come from people who went to a clinic. This study asks whether those clinic samples reflect what is actually spreading in the wider community, using data from Seattle-area community studies and Washington State clinical records. For RSV and influenza, the two sources looked similar; for COVID-19 during the pandemic, they differed in which variants were common and in the mutations seen.
summary.why: Genome sequencing guides decisions about vaccines, treatments and monoclonal antibodies, so knowing whether clinic-based samples miss important variants matters for surveillance budgets. The authors suggest that during pandemic-level spread, clinic-only sampling may miss variants, though the difference may partly reflect the much larger number of SARS-CoV-2 sequences and the effects of many co-circulating variants; the study is from one region and the authors call for testing elsewhere.

papers.abstract: BackgroundGenomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized. We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples. MethodsIn this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health. We compared clade proportions and dynamics, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values between clinical and community samples. FindingsWe analyzed 538 RSV sequences collected between 2019 and 2021 (278 community, 260 clinical), 1506 influenza sequences (260 community, 1246 clinical) between 2019 and 2020, and 8660 SARS-CoV-2 sequences (5923 community, 2737 clinical) from 2020 to 2022. Clade proportions did not differ between clinical and community samples for RSV or influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2: clades 21J (Delta) and 21K (Omicron BA.1) were more frequent in community samples and clade 22B (Omicron BA.5) in clinical samples. SARS-CoV-2 clinical sequence clusters were more diverse than community clusters, whereas RSV and influenza showed no significant difference. Several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples for SARS-CoV-2. Ct values were lower in clinical samples for multiple SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza clades. InterpretationSeasonal respiratory viruses had similar dynamics and diversity in clinical and community samples, whereas pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differed between settings. Genomic surveillance programs should combine clinical and community sampling, particularly during pandemics in order to better capture viral diversity. FundingThis analysis was funded by the Washington State Department of Health Northwest Pathogen Genomics Center of Excellence (WA DOH contract number HED29377-1, federal grant number NU50CK000630 to University of Washington). The underlying studies were funded by Gates Ventures. RESEARCH IN CONTEXTO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSGenomic surveillance of respiratory viruses expanded substantially during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since been extended to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza, but most sequences come from people who sought medical care. We searched PubMed for studies published in English up to September 2026 using combinations of terms "genomic surveillance", "community surveillance", "respiratory syncytial virus", "influenza", "SARS-CoV-2", "whole genome sequencing", and included studies that sequenced respiratory viruses from defined clinical or community populations. Previous work has sampled hospitalized patients, sequenced random positive specimens, or sequenced wastewater, and has shown that such data can track variant emergence, clade replacement, and nosocomial transmission. However, few studies compared clinical and community sampling for the same virus in the same population and period, so it remains unclear whether clinically derived sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to compare viral diversity between clinical and community sampling for three respiratory viruses in the same region and overlapping time periods. Using more than 10,000 whole genomes from community-based surveillance studies and state clinical surveillance in Washington State, we found that clade proportions and dynamics were similar between sources for RSV and influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2. At finer genetic resolution, clinical SARS-CoV-2 sequences formed more diverse clusters than community sequences, and several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples. Implications of all the available evidenceFor seasonal respiratory viruses, sampling people who seek care appears to capture much of the diversity circulating in the community, which may allow surveillance programs with limited resources to rely on clinical specimens. In contrast with seasonal circulation in a population with some pre-existing immunity, during pandemic-level transmission, when very large numbers of people in a largely susceptible population are infected over a short period, clinical and community samples are not interchangeable, and programs that sequence only clinical specimens risk missing variants circulating in the community, including mutations relevant to antiviral and monoclonal antibody resistance. These differences may partly reflect the much larger number of SARS-CoV-2 genomes available, as well as heterogeneous mixing and co-circulation of multiple variants during the pandemic. Surveillance programs should therefore combine clinical and community sampling, and future studies should test whether these patterns hold in other regions, seasons, and pathogens.
